recipes.title: Homemade Cottage Cheese
recipes.description: Simple large-curd cottage cheese made with milk and vinegar. Ready in about an hour, creamy texture with optional heavy cream.

instructions.text: Pour one gallon of milk into a large pot and heat to approximately 190°F, stirring gently with a wooden spoon to prevent burning.
Once the milk reaches 190°F, remove it from the stove immediately.
Add 3/4 cup of vinegar or lemon juice and stir. Cover the pot and let it rest for 30 minutes.
Line a colander with cheesecloth or a clean cotton towel and place it over a bowl.
Using a slotted spoon, transfer the curds from the pot into the lined colander. Let drain for 30 minutes.
Gather the cloth ends tightly, forming a ball. Run cold water over it while gently squeezing.
Place the cooled cheese in a bowl. Break it into smaller curds using a whisk or spoon, then stir in the salt.
Optional: Stir in heavy cream, two tablespoons at a time, until reaching desired creaminess.
Chill for at least one hour before serving. Use within 5-7 days.

notes: Rinsing curds with cold water reduces sourness
Do not overcook or curds will be tough
Can substitute apple cider vinegar or lemon juice for white vinegar
Store upside down in fridge to extend shelf life

recipes.title: Homemade Cream Cheese
recipes.description: Super easy 3-ingredient cream cheese ready in 10 minutes. Light, fluffy, and perfect for spreading or baking.

instructions.text: Pour milk into a saucepan and bring to a gentle simmer over medium-high heat for 1-2 minutes. Avoid a full boil.
Add lemon juice and stir with a wooden spoon, then turn off heat.
Set aside briefly while milk curdles - curds will form and yellowish whey will separate.
Pour curdled milk through cheesecloth and a sieve to remove whey.
Rinse the curds with cold water.
Squeeze curds thoroughly to remove remaining whey (reserve whey for other uses if desired).
Place strained curds in a food processor or blender with salt. Blend until light and fluffy.
Add 1-2 tbsp whey while blending if you prefer creamier texture.
Enjoy immediately or refrigerate up to 7 days. Can be frozen up to 2 months.

notes: UHT milk will not curdle properly
Lemon adds citrusy sweetness, vinegar creates more savory flavor
Avoid vigorous stirring - it breaks up curds
Can customize with herbs, pepper, or sweet chili

recipes.title: Queso Fresco
recipes.description: Latin American semi-soft cheese that can substitute for mozzarella. Lightly pressed and ready to eat in just a few days.

ingredients.item: goat or cow milk (raw or pasteurized)

instructions.text: Heat milk to 86°F (90°F for cow milk). Add mesophilic culture and lipase, stir thoroughly.
Allow to ripen for 1 hour.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk and stir vigorously for 15 seconds.
Cover and let sit 45 minutes until achieving a clean break, maintaining 86°F temperature.
Cut curds into 1/4-inch pieces. Rest undisturbed for 10 minutes.
Stir curds with wire whisk and gradually raise temperature to 95°F over 20 minutes, stirring occasionally. Let settle 5 minutes.
Drain whey (reserve for ricotta). Maintain curds at 95°F for 10 minutes while stirring.
Add salt and optional herbs (chives or jalapeños).
Line mold with cheesecloth. Add curds and press: 10 lbs for 10 minutes, flip, then 20 lbs for 1 hour, then 35 lbs for 6 hours.
Air dry overnight on a rack. Wrap and refrigerate several days before tasting.

notes: Raise all temperatures by 4°F if using cow milk instead of goat
Keeps refrigerated for several weeks
Does not freeze well
Can add chives or jalapeños for flavor

recipes.title: Panir / Queso Blanco
recipes.description: Simple acid-set cheese also called vinegar cheese. Bland, rubbery texture that doesn't melt - ideal as a meat substitute in curries, chili, or tacos.

instructions.text: Warm the milk to 183-185°F (not higher) and maintain that temperature for 10 minutes. Stir often to keep from scorching.
While stirring and keeping heat on, add vinegar gradually until curds separate. This should happen right away.
When curds separate cleanly from whey (fine white particles floating in greenish whey), pour into a cheesecloth-lined colander.
Tie the cloth corners together and hang the bag for several hours to drain.
Save the whey for later use. Refrigerate cheese; keeps approximately two weeks.

notes: Ideal beginner cheese requiring minimal equipment
Does not melt - use as meat substitute
Don't measure vinegar precisely - add until curds separate
Use cheesemaking grade cheesecloth, not grocery store variety

recipes.title: Traditional Ricotta (from Whey)
recipes.description: True ricotta made by re-cooking whey leftover from other cheeses. Uses heat to precipitate albumin protein. Mozzarella whey makes the best ricotta.

instructions.text: Heat whey to 200°F over direct heat.
Observe tiny white particles (albumin protein) forming.
Line colander with butter muslin or clean cotton cloth.
Carefully pour hot whey into lined colander over a pot.
Tie cloth ends and hang to drain for a couple hours.
Transfer ricotta to bowl, add salt to taste.
Refrigerate; keeps about 2 weeks.

notes: Omitting vinegar creates smoother texture
Different cheeses yield varying flavors - mozzarella makes the best
Not a high-yield cheese but worth the effort
True ricotta means 're-cooked' in Italian

recipes.title: Whole Milk Ricotta
recipes.description: Ricotta made directly from whole milk rather than whey. Drier and less creamy than traditional whey ricotta but more economical.

ingredients.item: white vinegar or fresh lemon juice

instructions.text: Heat milk to 200°F in heavy pot.
Add vinegar or lemon juice; return to 200°F.
Cover and rest undisturbed for 15 minutes.
Line colander with butter muslin or cotton cloth.
Pour hot mixture into lined colander.
Hang to drain 1+ hour (longer draining = drier cheese).
Break up, stir, and salt to taste.
Refrigerate; keeps about 1 week.

notes: Drier, less creamy than traditional whey ricotta
Economical alternative when you don't have whey
Drain longer for drier cheese suitable for baking

recipes.title: Cottage Cheese (Fias Co Farm Style)
recipes.description: Dry cottage cheese curds using mesophilic culture and rennet. Curds may be squeaky at first but lose their squeak with aging.

ingredients.item: goat or cow milk (raw, unpasteurized preferred)

instructions.text: Warm milk to 86°F (90°F for cow milk). Mix in mesophilic culture and let ripen for 1 hour.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk, stir vigorously for 15 seconds.
Cover and allow 45 minutes for a clean break while maintaining temperature.
Cut curds into approximately 1/2-inch pieces. Rest undisturbed for 10 minutes (5 minutes for cow milk).
Gently stir curds while gradually raising temperature to 95°F (99°F for cow milk) over 20 minutes.
Let settle 5 minutes. Drain whey to curd level.
Add cold water to lower temperature to 85°F, stir occasionally for 10 minutes.
Pour into colander and drain for about 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Separate curds into a bowl, salt to taste, cover, and refrigerate minimum 2 days.

recipes.temperature: 86°F initial (90°F for cow), raise to 95°F (99°F for cow)
notes: Curds may be squeaky at first but lose squeak with aging
Add cream before serving for creamier version
Raw unpasteurized milk preferred but pasteurized works

recipes.title: Homemade Mozzarella (Fias Co Farm)
recipes.description: Traditional stretched-curd mozzarella using citric acid for acidity development. Not recommended for beginners - the stretching technique takes practice.

ingredients.item: fresh goat or cow milk (not homogenized)

instructions.text: Sterilize all equipment. Pour milk into double boiler and add citric acid.
Warm milk to 91°F. Add culture and lipase, stir well.
Cover and let ripen for one hour at 90-91°F.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk and stir briskly for 15 seconds, then stop milk movement.
Cover and let set about 15 minutes until achieving a clean break.
Cut curds into 1/4-1/2 inch pieces using vertical, crosswise, then 45° angle cuts.
Let curds rest 10 minutes (5 minutes for cow milk).
Gently stir curds. Keep at 90-91°F, covered, for approximately one hour, stirring occasionally during first 30 minutes.
Allow curds to settle and mat together.
Pour curds into cheesecloth-lined colander. Tie ends and hang to drain 3-4 hours. Can refrigerate overnight.
Test readiness: cut small piece, place in 170°F water, check if it stretches without breaking.
Heat large pot of water to 170°F and add 1/2 cup kosher salt.
Cut curd into approximately 1-inch cubes.
Carefully add cubed curds to hot water. Stir carefully with slotted ladle.
Squeeze cubes to test - remove when soft throughout but not runny.
Transfer to large bowl. Gently form curds into one mass without squeezing.
Stretch and fold repeatedly, letting curd stretch under its own weight. Continue until smooth, shiny, and elastic (10-15 pulls).
Return cheese briefly to hot water to warm. Shape into ball or loaf.
Place in cold water (40°F) for approximately 1 hour to cool.
Refrigerate; use immediately or store up to 1 week. Freezes fairly well.

notes: Not recommended as first cheesemaking project
Acidity is what allows curds to stretch - no acidity, no stretch
Avoid overheating curds or they become runny with no recovery
Don't answer phone during curd working phase
One of few cheeses that freezes well

recipes.title: Chèvre / Fromage Blanc
recipes.description: Classic French soft goat cheese. Very simple to make with minimal equipment. Can be molded or made as bag cheese.

instructions.text: Sterilize all equipment. Warm milk to 72°F (or use freshly strained milk at natural temperature).
Add culture and stir well.
To measure 1/5 drop rennet: dilute 1 drop rennet in 5 tablespoons water, then use 1 tablespoon of this mixture. Stir thoroughly.
Cover pot and let sit undisturbed at ~72°F for 18-24 hours (can place in cold oven).
Milk will resemble thick yogurt when coagulated.
FOR FROMAGE BLANC (Bag Cheese): Pour curds into cheesecloth-lined colander, tie ends, hang to drain 6-8 hours. Salt to taste.
FOR MOLDED CHÈVRE: Pour off separated whey. Place molds on rack over pan. Ladle curds into molds, layering with herbs/pepper/garlic if desired. Drain 2 days at room temperature, covered.
Unmold carefully, salt all sides with kosher salt, wrap in plastic. Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated.

notes: Best served on crackers
Substitutes for cream cheese in recipes
Molds can be DIY using food-grade plastic containers with drainage holes
Fromage Blanc can be blended to sour cream texture

recipes.title: No-Rennet Queso Blanco
recipes.source_note: New Mexico State University Extension - pubs.nmsu.edu
recipes.description: Heat-acid white cheese made without culture or rennet. Semi-hard frying cheese that doesn't melt. Can be flavored with peppers, herbs, and spices.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 176°F for 20 minutes.
Mix vinegar with distilled water.
Slowly add vinegar mixture to hot milk until curds mat and become slightly stretchy (stretch about 0.39 inches before breaking).
Filter through cloth bag until whey drains.
Add salt and spices by kneading curds gently.
Press out remaining whey.
Place curds in boilable bags.
Seal bags and submerge in boiling water for 5 minutes.
Store refrigerated; consume fresh but keeps several weeks if properly sealed.

notes: Does not require culture or rennet
Frying cheese - does not melt
Can flavor with peppers, herbs, spices
Boiling in sealed bag extends shelf life

recipes.title: SAFE Queso Fresco
recipes.source_note: New Mexico State University Extension - pubs.nmsu.edu
recipes.description: Food-safe queso fresco recipe using buttermilk, vinegar, and rennet. Developed by university extension for home cheesemakers.

instructions.text: Combine buttermilk with milk.
Add vinegar and mix well.
Heat to 90°F; remove from heat.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk and mix 2 minutes.
Let stand 30-40 minutes until firm.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes; rest 5 minutes.
Heat curds to 115°F without stirring.
Remove from heat; rest 5 minutes.
Drain through cheesecloth 5 minutes.
Form curd ball; gently squeeze whey through cheesecloth.
Break curds into bowl; add salt.
Mix and rest 5 minutes; squeeze again.
Place in mold; refrigerate overnight.
Remove from mold; package in airtight container. Keep refrigerated.

notes: SAFE designation indicates food-safety tested recipe
Buttermilk provides both acid and culture
Use within 5-7 days

recipes.title: Homemade Cream Cheese (NMSU)
recipes.source_note: New Mexico State University Extension - pubs.nmsu.edu
recipes.description: Rich cream cheese using whole milk and whipping cream. University extension recipe with overnight draining.

instructions.text: Add milk, cream, and buttermilk to double boiler; warm to 85°F.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk and stir gently 4 minutes.
Cover and let stand 1 hour at 85°F until whey covers curd and breaks cleanly.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes; rest 5 minutes undisturbed.
Pour into cheesecloth-lined colander; refrigerate overnight.
Work 1.5 teaspoons salt into drained curds with wooden spoon.
Transfer to container or freezer bag.
Store refrigerated until use.

notes: Whipping cream adds richness
Can substitute plain yogurt for buttermilk
Overnight draining creates proper texture

recipes.title: Feta-Style Fresh Cheese
recipes.source_note: New Mexico State University Extension - pubs.nmsu.edu
recipes.description: Fresh feta-style cheese with hot brine treatment. Can be eaten fresh or aged, and seasoned with herbs, chile, or spices.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F over 30 minutes with occasional stirring.
Sprinkle culture over surface; let dissolve 2-4 minutes before stirring with 20 top-to-bottom strokes.
Let sit 2 hours.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk and stir with 15 top-to-bottom strokes.
Rest 7-10 minutes; check for clean break/custardy consistency.
Cut into 1/4-inch cubes; rest 10 minutes.
Stir gently 1 minute.
Allow curds to settle; remove and reserve whey.
Add salt to whey for 3.5% brine solution (8 tbsp per gallon); heat to 150°F.
Slowly add curds to hot brine 1 cup at a time over 15-20 minutes with gentle stirring.
Have cold distilled water available to cool curds to 118°F if needed.
Float curds in whey brine at 118°F for 15 minutes.
Transfer curds to plastic molds using perforated spoon; press lightly.
Remove from molds; cut into 1-inch chunks.
Add additional salt if desired (1 tsp per pound); season with herbs, chile, or spices.
Transfer to containers; eat fresh or age as desired.

notes: Hot brine treatment gives characteristic texture
Can eat fresh or age further
Season with herbs, chile, or spices
Non-homogenized milk recommended

recipes.title: Neufchâtel Cheese
recipes.source_note: New Mexico State University Extension - pubs.nmsu.edu
recipes.description: French-style soft cheese similar to cream cheese but with less fat. Can be made with any fat level milk.

ingredients.item: fresh cultured unsalted buttermilk (or plain yogurt)

instructions.text: Add milk to double boiler; stir in buttermilk or yogurt; warm to 92-94°F.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk and stir 2-3 minutes.
Let sit undisturbed 30 minutes at 92-94°F until firm gel forms.
Test by cutting slit with spatula; if curd breaks cleanly, ready to proceed.
Cut curd into 1-inch cubes; stir gently and continuously 20-30 minutes at 90-94°F to firm.
Pour off whey; allow curds to settle and dip out remaining whey.
Add 1 teaspoon salt; mix gently. Wait 5 minutes; add second teaspoon (optional). Wait 5 minutes; add third teaspoon (optional).
Divide curds into two batches.
Line two perforated containers with cheesecloth; fill with curds; fold cloth over top; add follower.
Apply pressure until surface is smooth (2-4 hours) allowing whey drainage.
Remove cheese and cloth; wrap tightly in plastic wrap.
Refrigerate; keeps 7-10 days or freezes 4-6 months.

notes: Minimum 1 tsp salt required for curd formation
Can use any fat level milk
Freezes well though quality reduces slightly
Similar to cream cheese but lower fat

recipes.title: Pizza Cheese (Mozzarella)
recipes.source_note: New Mexico State University Extension - pubs.nmsu.edu
recipes.description: Traditional stretched-curd mozzarella with yogurt culture. Includes detailed stretching and brining instructions for perfect pizza cheese.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 90°F; add yogurt; stir slowly 15 minutes at constant temperature.
Dissolve rennet in water. Add to milk and stir 3-5 minutes.
Cover at 90°F; let stand approximately 30 minutes until coagulated.
Cut curds into 1/2-inch cubes; rest 15 minutes with occasional stirring.
Slowly increase temperature to 118°F over 45 minutes; hold 15 additional minutes (total: 1 hour).
Allow curds to settle; remove whey; transfer curd mat to flat pan.
Turn curd mat every 15 minutes over 2 hours without cutting; mat should be tight when finished.
Cut mat into 1-2 inch wide strips.
Immerse strips in 180°F hot water; tumble and stretch using wooden spoons approximately 15 minutes until elastic.
Remove from hot water; hand-shape into ball or loaf.
Place in cold water (40°F) approximately 1 hour.
Prepare saturated salt brine (2 lbs salt per gallon water, keep at 40-50°F).
Immerse cheese in brine; cover exposed areas with dry salt; leave 24 hours.
Remove from brine; dry several hours; wrap in plastic.
Refrigerate; use immediately or store up to 1 week.

notes: Can blend 2 quarts whole milk with 2 quarts skim milk instead of 2%
Turning curd mat every 15 minutes is critical for texture
Saturated brine: some salt should remain undissolved
24-hour brining develops proper salt content

recipes.title: Homemade Cheddar Cheese
recipes.description: Traditional cloth-bound cheddar with the signature cheddaring process. Ages from 4-6 weeks for mild to 3+ months for sharp flavor.

instructions.text: Warm milk to 88°F, remove from heat.
Stir in culture and annatto; cover for 1 hour.
Add rennet, stir slowly for 30 seconds to stop milk motion.
Coagulate for 40-50 minutes using flocculation testing.
Cut curds to 1/4-inch pieces using grid and diagonal cuts.
Rest 5 minutes; slowly stir to find uncut pieces.
Warm to 95°F over 30 minutes with gradual stirring.
Increase heat to 102°F in 15 minutes; stir rapidly.
Maintain 102°F while stirring vigorously for 15 minutes.
Test: curds should hold together but break when rubbed.
Let curds settle 5-10 minutes; remove whey.
Cheddaring: Cut curd mass into 4 blocks; stack in pot within hot water bath.
Flip and restack every 15 minutes for 1 hour. Curds should reach cooked chicken breast consistency.
Weigh curds; calculate 2.6% salt amount.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes; add salt in two phases (5 minutes apart).
Transfer to cheesecloth-lined press; apply 20 lbs pressure for 15 minutes.
Flip, redress; apply 60 lbs overnight.
Final flip and redress; apply 80 lbs until 24 hours total pressing.
Air dry on mat for 2-3 days, flipping twice daily.
Brush cloth bandage with melted butter on top, bottom, and sides.
Age in cheese fridge at 55°F and 80% humidity: 4-6 weeks for mild, 3+ months for sharp.

notes: Use flocculation cap to test readiness rather than guessing
Don't dilute rennet in water
Maintain consistent 102°F temperature throughout cheddaring
Active stirring time approximately 1 hour; total preparation about 7 hours

recipes.title: Queso Blanco (Beginner Cheese)
recipes.description: A simple Latin American-style fresh cheese requiring no special equipment or ingredients. Perfect for beginners.

instructions.text: Heat milk in a large pot until it reaches about 180°F (just below boiling, small bubbles forming).
Remove from heat and slowly add vinegar while stirring gently.
Let sit for 10-15 minutes as curds form and separate from whey.
Line a colander with cheesecloth and strain the curds.
Let drain for 30 minutes or until desired consistency.
Season with salt if desired. Use fresh or refrigerate.

notes: Requires no special equipment or ingredients
Great for beginners
Yield depends on butterfat content of milk
Fresh cheese, use within 1 week

recipes.title: Whole Milk Ricotta
recipes.description: A high-yield ricotta using whole milk instead of whey. Makes enough to fill a lasagna pan.

instructions.text: Heat milk in a pot until small bubbles form around edges (about 180°F).
Remove from heat and add vinegar, stirring gently.
Let sit undisturbed for 5-10 minutes as curds form.
Line a strainer with cheesecloth and pour in curds.
Let drain for 30-60 minutes depending on desired consistency.
Season with salt and use in recipes or refrigerate.

notes: Unlike traditional ricotta using whey, this whole milk version produces enough cheese to make lasagna
Adjust vinegar amount if curds don't form well
Longer draining produces drier ricotta

recipes.title: Easy Mozzarella (Beginner-Friendly)
recipes.description: A forgiving mozzarella recipe for beginners using citric acid and rennet. Video tutorials available.

instructions.text: Dissolve citric acid in 1/4 cup water.
Pour milk into large pot and add citric acid solution while stirring.
Heat milk to 90°F while stirring gently.
Dissolve rennet in 1/4 cup water.
Remove pot from heat and add rennet solution, stirring for 30 seconds.
Cover and let sit 5-10 minutes until a clean break is achieved.
Cut curds into 1-inch cubes.
Return to low heat and slowly warm to 105°F while gently stirring.
Remove curds with slotted spoon to microwave-safe bowl.
Microwave for 1 minute, drain whey, and knead.
Microwave 30 seconds more, add salt, and stretch until smooth and shiny.
Form into ball and place in ice water to set shape.

notes: Recipe is incredibly forgiving for newcomers
Do not use ultra-pasteurized milk
If curds don't form, try adding more rennet
Mistakes happen to all cheesemakers - persistence pays off

recipes.title: Two-Ingredient Homestead Cheese
recipes.description: The simplest possible cheese using just milk and acid. Perfect for using up excess milk from homesteading. Whey byproduct has multiple uses.

ingredients.item: fresh milk (goat, cow, pasteurized, or raw)
apple cider vinegar (or white vinegar, lemon juice)

instructions.text: In a large pot, heat the milk slowly, stirring occasionally to prevent burning.
Heat until reaching approximately 175°F (milk will begin to froth).
Keep the heat on, add the apple cider vinegar and stir until the milk curdles.
Continue to stir the curds gently for about 10 minutes as they develop.
Using a strainer, collect the solid curds out of the remaining liquid (whey).
For maximum dryness, transfer to cheesecloth and hang. Otherwise, let drain in strainer for at least 30 minutes.
Season with salt and herbs if desired.

notes: Fresh milk from homesteading adds up quickly - cheese is a great way to use it
Whey can be used in baking, smoothies, soups, or fed to pets
Vinegar amount can range from a few tablespoons to 1/2 cup depending on milk
Works with any type of fresh milk

recipes.title: Farmer's Cheese (Tvorog)
recipes.description: Traditional Eastern European farmer's cheese (tvorog). A simple, tangy fresh cheese used in cooking and baking.

instructions.text: Heat 1 gallon milk over medium-low until you see hundreds of little bubbles appear, but do not bring to a boil (30-40 minutes). Stir occasionally to prevent scorching.
Once you see lots of bubbles popping, slowly add 1/2 cup distilled white vinegar.
Give it a gentle stir and wait for 30-60 seconds. Then stir again.
The cheese will curdle (become crumbly) and the water should be lime/yellow-ish color. Add more vinegar if needed.
Cool to room temperature.
Line a sieve or colander with a flour sack towel.
Slowly pour the cheese into the cloth to catch the curds.
Gather the cloth around cheese and squeeze as much as you can to get all the whey out. Stop when white-ish liquid appears.
Refrigerate once cooled. Keep in refrigerator for up to a week.

notes: Traditional Eastern European cheese
Used in blintzes, pierogi, and desserts
Squeeze until white liquid appears - that means you've removed enough whey
Heinz brand vinegar specifically recommended

recipes.title: Homemade Gouda Cheese
recipes.description: A washed-curd Dutch cheese known for its natural sweetness. The washing step lowers milk sugar, reducing acid and producing a mild, creamy cheese.

instructions.text: Heat milk to 84°F.
Add culture, let sit 15 minutes to ripen.
Add diluted calcium chloride (if using pasteurized milk).
Add diluted rennet, stir 30 seconds.
Heat water to 140°F separately.
Wait 25-30 minutes for clean break, then cut curds slowly into pea-sized pieces over 10 minutes.
Drain 1/4 of the whey.
Add 140°F water until curds reach 90°F (this is the 'washing' step).
Stir gently for 12 minutes.
Drain whey to half original volume.
Add more water until curds reach 95°F.
Stir 10 minutes. Drain completely.
Transfer curds to mold.
Press at 15 lbs for 30 minutes, flip, press another 30 minutes.
After 12 hours, submerge in refrigerated brine overnight.
Remove, pat dry, place on mat at room temperature.
Turn regularly until dry (about 5 days).
Vacuum seal or wax.
Age minimum 2 months at 50-55°F with 75-95% humidity.

recipes.temperature: 84°F initial, 90°F first wash, 95°F second wash, 50-55°F aging
notes: Gouda's defining feature is its natural sweetness from the washing step
Washing curds replaces whey with hot water, lowering milk sugar and reducing acid
Digital thermometer accuracy is critical
Wax or vacuum seal for aging

recipes.title: Traditional Gouda Cheese
recipes.description: A traditional washed-curd gouda with proper pressing weights and extended aging. Features Flora Danica culture for authentic flavor.

instructions.text: Warm milk to 32°C (90°F).
Add Flora Danica culture and stir thoroughly.
Cover and ripen for 15 minutes.
Add diluted rennet and let set 45 minutes to 1 hour until clean break achieved.
Cut curds into 1cm cubes.
Rest 10 minutes.
Pour off one-third of whey.
Slowly add 80°C (175°F) water until temperature reaches 33°C (92°F).
Stir continuously, rest 10 minutes.
Drain whey to curd level.
Add more 80°C water until reaching 38°C (100°F).
Rest 30 minutes.
Drain all remaining whey.
Transfer curds gently to cloth-lined mold (avoid breaking curds).
Press at 10kg for 30 minutes; flip and redress.
Press at 20kg for 30 minutes; flip and redress.
Press at 25kg for 12 hours.
Unwrap cheese.
Soak in saturated brine 12 hours, turning every 3 hours.
Pat dry and air dry at 10°C for 3 weeks.
Wax and age at 10°C for 3-9 months.
Turn cheese 3-4 times weekly during aging.

recipes.temperature: 32°C (90°F) initial, 33°C (92°F) first wash, 38°C (100°F) second wash, 10°C aging
notes: Flora Danica culture provides authentic Dutch flavor
Increasing press weights (10kg, 20kg, 25kg) develops proper texture
Turn cheese frequently during aging
Cheese improves with longer aging - patience pays off

recipes.title: Homemade Halloumi Cheese
recipes.description: A quick halloumi using the microwave method. Ready in about an hour. Features the traditional herbs and high melting point for grilling.

instructions.text: Combine both milks in a large saucepan.
Dissolve the junket tablet in 1 tablespoon water.
Heat milk to 32-35°C (89.5-95°F), then remove from heat and add dissolved junket. Stir briefly.
Set aside for 30 minutes in a warm place. The milk should set and become jelly-like.
Cut the set milk into curds using a wooden spoon to separate the whey.
Transfer to a microwave-safe bowl with herbs and chilli. Wait 10 minutes.
Microwave on high for 2 minutes, stir, then heat another 2 minutes.
Test curds—they should be elastic and slightly firm. Heat 1 more minute if needed.
Line a fine sieve with gauze over a bowl. Strain curds, reserving 1/2 cup whey for brine.
Sprinkle salt over curds, mix, and press to remove excess whey.
Gather gauze edges and squeeze additional whey out.
Combine all brine ingredients and mix well.
Press cheese into a rectangular container. Refrigerate or freeze 15 minutes to cool.
Transfer to a larger container and cover with brine. Store in refrigerator for a couple of days.

notes: Halloumi has a high melting point - perfect for grilling or frying
Mix of cow and goat milk is traditional
Store in brine to preserve
Best grilled or pan-fried while fresh

recipes.title: Homemade Blue Cheese
recipes.description: An advanced blue cheese using Penicillium Roqueforti. Requires needling to create characteristic blue veins. Ages 90+ days.

instructions.text: Warm milk to 30°C (86°F).
Add cultures (mesophilic and Penicillium Roqueforti) and stir thoroughly.
Ripen for 1.5 hours.
Add diluted rennet and let set for 1 hour until clean break achieved.
Carefully cut the curd into fine, pea-sized pieces.
Over 60 minutes, stir the curds every 5 minutes while maintaining temperature.
Drain curds through cheesecloth.
Salt the curds and transfer to molds.
Turn molds every 15 minutes for the first hour, then hourly for three more hours.
Store overnight at 80% humidity and 20°C.
For the next 14 days, rotate and turn the cheese stack daily at 95% humidity and 10°C.
Rub with salt for the first week only.
After 4-10 days of visible mold, pierce the cheese with a stainless-steel needle at 2.5cm intervals.
This needling creates air holes allowing oxygen inside, forming the characteristic blue veins.
Ripen for 90 additional days at 95% humidity and 10°C.
Turn every 3-4 days and scrape surface mold.
Finally, wrap in foil and store at 8°C.

notes: Advanced recipe - not for beginners
Needling is critical: pierce at 2.5cm intervals to allow oxygen penetration
The blue veins form along needle paths where oxygen enters
Only a tiny speck of Penicillium Roqueforti is needed
95% humidity is essential during aging
